title: Learning the language of antibody hypervariability
one_line: AbMAP is a transfer-learning framework that adapts general protein language models to antibody hypervariable regions (CDRs) via in silico mutation-based contrastive augmentation and multitask structure/function supervision.
key_claims: Focusing representations on CDRs while inheriting knowledge from foundational protein language models outperforms both general-purpose and antibody-only models.
In optimizing SARS-CoV-2-binding antibodies, AbMAP-guided designs achieved an 82% hit rate.
Designed variants showed up to 22-fold increases in binding affinity, and the model predicted both strong and weak binders.
Applied to B-cell receptor repertoires, AbMAP revealed structural/functional convergence across individuals, with repertoires more similar in function than in sequence.
Therapeutic antibodies cluster in specific regions of AbMAP's representation space, and the framework is model-agnostic so it can adopt future PLMs.
limitations: Balancing framework-region versus hypervariable-region contributions to the representation remains unresolved.
Contrastive augmentation via in silico mutagenesis carries a computational efficiency cost.
Validation centred on SARS-CoV-2 antibody optimization rather than diverse target classes.
Not demonstrated at the scale of industrial antibody development pipelines.
Show notes report hit rate and fold-affinity gains without the number of designs tested or baseline comparators.
open_questions: Prospective head-to-head design campaigns against established computational and experimental affinity-maturation methods on multiple antigens.
Whether AbMAP gains persist when built on newer, larger protein language models.
Whether functional convergence seen in repertoire space predicts shared antigen specificity experimentally.
Whether representation-space proximity to therapeutic antibodies predicts developability or clinical success.
